Another argument may be added, — though we may be pressed down by adversity, yet we are not excluded from the number of God’s children, since we see him going before us who was by nature his only Son; for that we are counted his children is owing only to the gift of adoption by which he admits us into a union with him, who alone lays claim to this honor in his own right.<div eID="gen132553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132554" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">When he had offered up prayers,</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> The second thing he mentions respecting Christ is, that he, as it became him, sought a remedy that he might be delivered from evils; and he said this that no one might think that Christ had an iron heart which felt nothing; for we ought always to consider why a thing is said. Had Christ been touched by no sorrow, no consolation could arise to us from his sufferings; but when we hear that he also endured the bitterest agonies of mind, the likeness becomes then evident to us. Christ, he says, did not undergo death and other evils because he disregarded them or was pressed down by no feeling of distress, but he prayed with tears, by which he testified the extreme anguish of his soul. <note n="87"> <div sID="gen132555" type="x-p"/> “Prayers and supplications” are nearly of the same meaning; the first word means a request, a petition, strictly a prayer; and the last an earnest or humble entreaty. The last word is found only here in the New Testament; once in the Septuagint, in <reference osisRef="Bible:Job.41.3">Job 41:3</reference>; and once in the Apocrypha, <reference osisRef="Bible:2Macc.9.18">2 Macc. 9:18</reference>. Hesychius, as quoted by Schleusner, gives παράκλησις, request, entreaty, as its meaning: it comes from ἱκέτης, a suppliant. The word ἱκετηρία, which is here used means first an olive branch wrapped in wool, carried by suppliants as a symbol of entreaty and hence used often in the sense of entreaty and supplication. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen132555" type="x-p"/> </note> Then by <hi type="italic">tears</hi> and <hi type="italic">strong crying</hi> the Apostle meant to express the intensity of his grief, for it is usual to show it by outward symptoms; nor do I doubt but that he refers to that prayer which the Evangelists mention, “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.26.42">Matthew 26:42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.22.42">Luke 22:42</reference>;) and also to another, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.27.46">Matthew 27:46</reference>.) For in the second instance mention is made by the evangelists of strong crying; and in the first it is not possible to believe that his eyes were dry, since drops of blood, through excessive grief, flowed from his body. It is indeed certain that he was reduced to great straits; and being overwhelmed with real sorrows, he earnestly prayed his Father to bring him help. <note n="88"> <div sID="gen132556" type="x-p"/> Stuart on this passage very justly observes, “If Jesus died as a common virtuous suffered, and merely as a martyr to the truth, without any vicarious suffering laid upon him, then is his death a most unaccountable event in respect to the manner of his behavior while suffering it; and it must be admitted that multitudes of humble, sinful, meek and very imperfect disciples of Christianity have surpassed their Master in the fortitude, and collected firmness and calm complacency which are requisite to triumph over the pangs of a dying hour. But who can well believe this? Or who can regard Jesus as a simple sufferer in the ordinary way upon the cross, and explain the mysteries of his dreadful horror before and during the hours of crucifixion?”<div eID="gen132556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132557" type="x-p"/>What is referred to is certainly inexplicable, except we admit what is often and in various ways plainly taught us in God’s word, that Christ died for our sins. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen132557" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen132554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132558" type="x-p"/>And what application is to be made of this? Even this, that whenever our evils press upon us and overwhelm us, we may call to mind the Son of God who labored under the same; and since he has gone before us there is no reason for us to faint. We are at the same time reminded that deliverance from evils can be found from no other but from God alone, and what better guidance can we have as to prayer than the example of Christ? He betook himself immediately to the Father. And thus the Apostle indicates what ought to be done by us when he says that he offered prayers to him who was able to deliver him from death; for by these words he intimates that he rightly prayed, because he fled to God the only Deliverer. His <hi type="italic">tears</hi> and <hi type="italic">crying</hi> recommend to us ardor and earnestness in prayer, for we ought not to pray to God formally, but with ardent desires.<div eID="gen132558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132559" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">And was heard,</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> Some render the following words, “on account of his reverence” or fears but I wholly differ from them. In the first place he puts the word alone ἐυλαθείας without the possessive “his”; and then there is the preposition ἀπὸ “from,” not ὑπὲρ “on account of,” or any other signifying a cause or a reason. As, then, εὐλάθεια means for the most part fear or anxiety, I doubt not but that the Apostle means that Christ was heard from that which he feared, so that he was not overwhelmed by his evils or swallowed up by death. For in this contest the Son of God had to engage, not because he was tried by unbelief, the source of all our fears, but because he sustained as a man in our flesh the judgment of God, the terror of which could not have been overcome without an arduous effort. Chrysostom interprets it of Christ’s dignity, which the Father in a manner reverenced; but this cannot be admitted. Others render it “piety.” But the explanation I have given is much more suitable, and requires no long arguments in its favor. <note n="89"> <div sID="gen132560" type="x-p"/> The idea of the effect of hearing, that is deliverance, is no doubt included in εἰσακουσθεὶς, “having been heard,” as it is sometimes in the corresponding word in Hebrew; so that Stuart is justified in the rendering it delivered, — “and being delivered from that which he feared.” It is rendered the same by Macknight, “and being delivered from fear.” Both Beza and Grotius render the last word fear; and this is its meaning as used in the Septuagint. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen132560" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen132559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132561" type="x-p"/>Now he added this third particular, lest we should think that Christ’s prayers were rejected, because he was not immediately delivered from his evils; for at no time was God’s mercy and aid wanting to him. And hence we may conclude that God often hears our prayers, even when that is in no way made evident. For though it belongs not to us to prescribe to him as it were a fixed rule, nor does it become him to grant whatsoever requests we may conceive in our minds or express with our tongues, yet he shows that he grants our players in everything necessary for our salvation. So when we seem apparently to be repulsed, we obtain far more than if he fully granted our requests.<div eID="gen132561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132562" type="x-p"/>But how was Christ heard from what he feared, as he underwent the death which he dreaded? To this I reply, that we must consider what it was that he feared; why was it that he dreaded death except that he saw in it the curse of God, and that he had to wrestle with the guilt of all iniquities, and also with hell itself? Hence was his trepidation and anxiety; for extremely terrible is God’s judgment. He then obtained what he prayed for, when he came forth a conqueror from the pains of death, when he was sustained by the saving hand of the Father, when after a short conflict he gained a glorious victory over Satan, sin, and hell. Thus it often happens that we ask this or that, but not for a right end; yet God, not granting what we ask, at the same time finds out himself a way to succor us.<div eID="gen132562" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.5.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen132549" osisID="Heb.5.7" type="section"/>
entries.de78eef6a12cacd1a4b756c6f989999a911b21db: <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.5.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Heb.5.8" sID="gen132563" type="section"/> <div sID="gen132564" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> <hi type="italic">Yet learned he obedience,</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> The proximate end of Christ’s sufferings was thus to habituate himself to obedience; not that he was driven to this by force, or that he had need of being thus exercised, as the case is with oxen or horses when their ferocity is to be tamed, for he was abundantly willing to render to his Father the obedience which he owed. But this was done from a regard to our benefit, that he might exhibit to us an instance and an example of subjection even to death itself. It may at the same time be truly said that Christ by his death learned fully what it was to obey God, since he was then led in a special manner to deny himself; for renouncing his own will, he so far gave himself up to his Father that of his own accord and willingly he underwent that death which he greatly dreaded. The meaning then is that Christ was by his sufferings taught how far God ought to be submitted to and obeyed.<div eID="gen132564" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132565" type="x-p"/>It is then but right that we also should by his example be taught and prepared by various sorrows, and at length by death itself, to render obedience to God; nay, much more necessary is this in our case, for we have a disposition contumacious and ungovernable until the Lord subdues us by such exercises to bear his yoke. This benefit, which arises from the cross, ought to allay its bitterness in our hearts; for what can be more desirable than to be made obedient to God? But this cannot be effected but by the cross, for in prosperity we exult as with loose reins; nay, in most cases, when the yoke is shaken off, the wantonness of the flesh breaks forth into excesses. But when restraint is put on our will, when we seek to please God, in this act only does our obedience show itself; nay, it is an illustrious proof of perfect obedience when we choose the death to which God may call us, though we dread it, rather than the life which we naturally desire.<div eID="gen132565" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.5.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen132563" osisID="Heb.5.8" type="section"/>
entries.eb431bd3efa060b24ceec99d3850cd4c752fba7c: <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.5.9" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Heb.5.9" sID="gen132566" type="section"/> <div sID="gen132567" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">9.</hi> <hi type="italic">And being made perfect, </hi>or <hi type="italic">sanctified, etc.</hi> Here is the ultimate or the remoter end, as they call it, why it was necessary for Christ to suffer: it was that he might thus become initiated into his priesthood, as though the Apostle had said that the enduring of the cross and death were to Christ a solemn kind of consecration, by which he intimates that all his sufferings had a regard to our salvation. It hence follows, that they are so far from being prejudicial to his dignity that they are on the contrary his glory; for if salvation be highly esteemed by us, how honorably ought we to think of its cause or author? For he speaks not here of Christ only as an example, but he ascends higher, even that he by his obedience has blotted out our transgressions. He became then the cause of salvation, because he obtained righteousness for us before God, having removed the disobedience of Adam by an act of an opposite kind, even obedience.<div eID="gen132567" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132568" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Sanctified</hi> suits the passage better than “made perfect.” The Greek word τελειωθεὶς means both; but as he speaks here of the priesthood, he fitly and suitably mentions sanctification. And so Christ himself speaks in another place, “For their sakes I sanctify myself.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.17.19">John 17:19</reference>.) It hence appears that this is to be properly applied to his human nature, in which he performed the office of a priest, and in which he also suffered. <note n="90"> <div sID="gen132569" type="x-p"/> The word τελειωθεὶς, means here the same as in <reference osisRef="Bible:Heb.2.10">chapter 2:10</reference>. Stuart gives it the same meaning here as in the former passage, “Then when exalted to glory,” etc.; but this does not comport with what follows, for it was not his exaltation to glory that qualified him to be “the author (or the causer or effecter) of eternal salvation,” but his perfect or complete work in suffering, by his having completely and perfectly performed the work of atonement. And that his suffering in obedience to God’s will, even his vicarious suffering, is meant here, appears also from the following reference to his being a priest after the order of Melchisedec. The meaning then seems to be, that Christ having fully completed his work as a priest, and that by suffering, became thereby the author of eternal salvation. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen132569" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen132568" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132570" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">To all them that obey him.</hi> If then we desire that Christ’s obedience should be profitable to us, we must imitate him; for the Apostle means that its benefit shall come to none but to those who obey. But by saying this he recommends faith to us; for he becomes not ours, nor his blessings, except as far as we receive them and him by faith. He seems at the same time to have adopted a universal term, <hi type="italic">all,</hi> for this end, that he might show that no one is precluded from salvation who is but teachable and becomes obedient to the Gospel of Christ.<div eID="gen132570" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.5.9" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen132566" osisID="Heb.5.9" type="section"/>
entries.fb39ccc207b7db2663f1790503feb5832c327b8e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.5.10" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Heb.5.10" sID="gen132571" type="section"/> <div sID="gen132572" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">10.</hi> <hi type="italic">Called of God,</hi> or <hi type="italic">named by God, etc.</hi> As it was necessary that he should pursue more at large the comparison between Christ and Melchisedec, on which he had briefly touched, and that the mind of the Jews should be stirred up to greater attention, he so passes to a digression that he still retails his argument.<div eID="gen132572" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.5.10" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen132571" osisID="Heb.5.10" type="section"/>
entries.602656c2d983338e4bda7b224c9f0209c842f7dd:
11. He therefore makes a preface by saying that he had many things to say, but that they were to prepare themselves lest these things should be said in vain. He reminds them that they were hard or difficult things; not indeed to repel them, but to stimulate them to greater attention. For as things that are easily understood render us slothful, so we become more keenly bent on hearing when anything obscure is set before us. He however states that the cause of the difficulty was not in the subject but in themselves. And indeed the Lord speaks to us so clearly and without any obscurity, that his word is rightly called our light; but its brightness become dim through our darkness.
The literal rendering is “Of whom we have many a word to say, and hardly explainable,” or hard to be explained. This hardness of explanation was however owing to their dullness of comprehension, as Calvin justly observes. “Hard to be uttered” of our version is not correct; nor is “hard to be understood” of Doddridge right. Macknight gives the true meaning, “difficult to be explained.” Beza’s is the same. The reason is added “Since dull (or sluggish) ye are become in ears,” or in hearings. To be dull in ears is to be inattentive; but to be sluggish in ears seems to mean stupidity, slowness of comprehension. The latter is evidently meant here; that is, a tardiness or slowness in understanding. To hear with the ear is in the language of Scripture to understand. (Matthew 11:15; John 8:43; 1 Corinthians 14:2.) Hence to be sluggish in ears is to be slow or tardy in understanding the Word of God. Stuart therefore gives the sense, “Since ye are dull of apprehension.” — Ed.
This happens partly through our dullness and partly through our sloth; for though we are very dull to understand the truth of God, yet there is to be added to this vice the depravity of our affections, for we apply our minds to vanity rather than to God’s truth. We are also continually impeded either by our perverseness, or by the cares of the world, or by the lusts of our flesh. Of whom does not refer to Christ, but to Melchisedec; yet he is not referred to as a private man, but as the type of Christ, and in a manner personating him.
Hebrews Chapter 5:12-14
12. For when for the time ye ought to be teachers, ye have need that one teach you again which be the first principles of the oracles of God; and are become such as have need of milk, and not of strong meat.
12. Nam quum debeatis esse doctores pro ratione temporis, rursum opus habetis, ut quis vos doceat elementa initii sermonum Dei; et facti estis ii quibus lacte opus sit et non solido cibo.
13. For every one that useth milk is unskillful in the word of righteousness: for he is a babe.
13. Nam quisquis lactis est particeps, imperitus est sermonis justitae, infans est enim.
14. But strong meat belongeth to them that are of full age, even those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
14. Perfectorum vero est solidus cibus, qui propter assuetudinem sensus habent exercitatos ad discretionem boni et mali.
entries.df0d3bac71ac199e22415f7fa5dbd012621306e5: <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.5.12" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Heb.5.12" sID="gen132585" type="section"/> <div sID="gen132586" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">12.</hi> <hi type="italic">For when for the time ye ought,</hi> <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> This reproof contains in it very sharp goads to rouse the Jews from their sloth. He says that it was unreasonable and disgraceful that they should still continue in the elements, in the first rudiments of knowledge, while they ought to have been teachers. “You ought,” he says, “to have been the instructors of others, but ye are not even disciples capable of comprehending an ordinary truth; for ye do not as yet understand the first rudiments of Christianity.” That he might, however, make them the more ashamed of themselves, he mentions the “first principles,” or the elements of the beginning of God’s words, as though he had said, You do not know the alphabet. We must, indeed, learn through life; for he alone is truly wise who owns that he is very far from perfect knowledge; but we ought still to profit so much by learning as not to continue always in the first principles. Nor are we to act in such a way, that what is said by Isaiah should be verified in us,<div eID="gen132586" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132587" type="x-p"/>“There shall be to you a precept on precept, a precept on precept,” <hi type="italic">etc.</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.10">Isaiah 28:10</reference>;)<div eID="gen132587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132588" type="x-p"/>but we ought, on the contrary, so to exert ourselves, that our progress may correspond to<hi type="italic"> the time</hi> allowed us.<div eID="gen132588" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132589" type="x-p"/>Doubtless, not only years, but days also, must be accounted for; so that every one ought to strive to make progress; but few there are who summon themselves to an account as to past time, or who show any concern for the future. We are, therefore, justly punished for our sloth, for most of us remain in elements fitted for children. We are further reminded, that it is the duty of every one to impart the knowledge he has to his brethren; so that no one is to retain what he knows to himself, but to communicate it to the edification of others. <note n="92"> <div sID="gen132590" type="x-p"/> Our version of this clause is very literal and compact, and sufficiently plain, “For when for the time ye ought to be teachers.” Its elegance and conciseness are not retained either by Macknight or by Stuart. What is implied in the words, “for the time,” is sufficiently evident without being expressed. As to the following sentence, “Ye have need,” etc., some difficulty has been found in the construction. I render it as follows, “Ye have again need of this — that some one should teach you the first principles of the oracles of God.” I take τίνα to be accusative before “teach.” The word “oracles” is used by Peter in the same sense, as designating the doctrines of the Gospels, <reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.4.11">1 Peter 4:11</reference>. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi><div eID="gen132590" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen132589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132591" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">Such as have need of milk.</hi> Paul uses the same metaphor in <reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.3.2">1 Corinthians 3:2</reference>; and he reproaches the Corinthians with the same fault with what is mentioned here, at least with one that is very similar; for he says, that they were carnal and could not bear solid food. Milk then means an elementary doctrine suitable to the ignorant. Peter takes the word in another sense, when he bids us to desire the milk that is without deceit, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.2.2">1 Peter 2:2</reference>;) for there is a twofold childhood, that is, as to wickedness, and as to understanding; and so Paul tells us, “Be not children in understanding, but in wickedness.” (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.14.20">1 Corinthians 14:20</reference>.) They then who are so tender that they cannot receive the higher doctrine, are by way of reproach called children.<div eID="gen132591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen132592" type="x-p"/>For the right application of doctrines is to join us together, so that we may grow to a perfect manhood, to the measure of full age, and that we should not be like children, tossed here and there, and carried about by every wind of doctrine. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.4.14">Ephesians 4:14</reference>.) We must indeed show some indulgence to those who have not yet known much of Christ, if they are not capable as yet of receiving <hi type="italic">solid food,</hi> but he who has had time to grow, if he till continues a child, is not entitled to any excuse. We indeed see that Isaiah brands the reprobate with this mark, that they were like children newly weaned from the breasts. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.28.9">Isaiah 28:9</reference>.) The doctrine of Christ does indeed minister milk to babes as well as strong meat to adults; but as the babe is nourished by the milk of its nurse, not that it may ever depend on the breast, but that it may by degrees grow and take stronger food; so also at first we must suck milk from Scripture, so that we may afterwards feed on its bread. The Apostle yet so distinguishes between milk and strong food, that he still understands sound doctrine by both, but the ignorant begin with the one, and they who are well­taught are strengthened by the other.<div eID="gen132592" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.5.12" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen132585" osisID="Heb.5.12" type="section"/>
entries.eeab6d9e382b6f1a5628f3602711dad5f3d7dcd1: <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.5.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Heb.5.13" sID="gen132593" type="section"/> <div sID="gen132594" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">For every one who uses milk,</hi> or, <hi type="italic">who partakes of milk, etc.</hi> He means those who from tenderness or weakness as yet refuse solid doctrine; for otherwise he who is grown up is not averse to milk. But he reproves here an infancy in understanding, such as constrains God even to prattle with us. He then says, that babes are not fit to receive the <hi type="italic">word of righteousness,</hi> understanding by righteousness the perfection of which he will presently speak. <note n="93"> <div sID="gen132595" type="x-p"/> This is the view of Grotius and others, but some regard “the word of righteousness” as a paraphrasis for the Gospel; and Stuart renders it, “the word of salvation.” Dr. Owen says that the Gospel is called “the word of righteousness,” because it reveals the righteousness of God, <reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.1.17">Romans 1:17</reference>. It may also be so called, because it reveals and contains the truth, the full truth, partly revealed previously. The word “righteousness” has this meaning both in the Old and New Testaments. See <reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.3.4">Psalm 3:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Isa.45.19 Bible:Isa.45.23">Isaiah 45:19, 23</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.21.23">Matthew 21:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.11.15">2 Corinthians 11:15</reference>. “The ministers of righteousness” in the last text are opposed to false ministers. — <hi type="italic">Ed</hi>.<div eID="gen132595" type="x-p"/> </note> For the Apostle does not here, as I think, refer to the question, how we are justified before God, but takes the word in a simpler sense, as denoting that completeness of knowledge which leads to perfection, which office Paul ascribes to the Gospel in his epistle to the <reference osisRef="Bible:Col.1.28">Colossians, 1:28</reference>; as though he had said, that those who indulge themselves in their ignorance preclude themselves from a real knowledge of Christ, and that the doctrine of the Gospel is unfruitful in them, because they never reach the goal, nor come even near it.<div eID="gen132594" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Heb.5.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen132593" osisID="Heb.5.13" type="section"/>
entries.185560d731fcd756d3f39f87260de4569072cda7:
14. Of full age, or perfect, etc. He calls those perfect who are adults; he mentions them in opposition to babes, as it is done in 1 Corinthians 2:6; 14:20; Ephesians 4:13. For the middle and manly age is the full age of human life; but he calls those by a figure men in Christ; who are spiritual. And such he would have all Christians to be, such as have attained by continual practice a habit to discern between good and evil. For he cannot have been otherwise taught aright in the truth, except we are fortified by his protection against all the falsehoods and delusions of Satan; for on this account it is called the sword of the Spirit. And Paul points out this benefit conferred by sound doctrine when he says, “That we may not be carried about by every wind of doctrine.” (Ephesians 4:14.) And truly what sort of faith is that which doubts, being suspended between truth and falsehood? Is it not in danger of coming to nothing every moment?
But not satisfied to mention in one word the mind, he mentions all the senses, in order to show that we are ever to strive until we be in every way furnished by God’s word, and be so armed for battle, that Satan may by no means steal upon us with his fallacies.
The word for “senses” means literally the organs of the senses, such as the eyes, the ears, etc., but here as signifying the senses themselves, as seeing, hearing, tasting, and smelling, by means of which those grown up are enabled by long experience to know what is good and wholesome for them, and also what is bad and injurious. By this comparison, which is here carried out fully, he intimates that the grown up in Christian truth attain by the habit of exercising all the senses or faculties of their minds, a capacity to distinguish between good and evil, between truth and error, in religion.
The doctrine of reserve cannot be drawn from this passage; for though the Apostle says that they were not capable, owing to their sloth, or taking strong food, he yet lays it before them. — Ed.
It hence appears what sort of Christianity there is under the Papacy, where not only the grossest ignorance is commended under the name of simplicity, but where the people are also most rigidly prevented from seeking real knowledge; nay, it is easy to judge by what spirit they are influenced, who hardly allow that to be touched which the Apostle commands us to handle continually, who imagine that a laudable neglect which the Apostle here so severely reproves, who take away the word of God, the only rule of discerning rightly, which discerning he declares to be necessary for all Christians! But among those who are freed from this diabolical prohibition and enjoy the liberty of learning, there is yet often no less indifference both as to hearing and reading. When thus we exercise not our powers, we are stupidly ignorant and void of all discernment.
CHAPTER 6
Hebrews Chapter 6:1-2
1. Therefore leaving the principles of the doctrine of Christ, let us go on unto perfection; not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works, and of faith toward God,
1. Quare omisso sermone principii Christi, ad perfectionem feramur, non jacentes rursum fundamentum poenitentiae ab operibus mortuis et fidei in Deum.
2. Of the doctrine of baptisms, and of laying on of hands, and of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.
2. (Baptismatum doctrinae et impositionis manuum) et resurrectionis mortuorum et judicii aeterni.

What those Sacrifices were which would please him, God only could reveal, as who should offer them both for himself and others; and this he did reveal to <ns0:hi>Adam, Noah,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Abraham,</ns0:hi> and to <ns0:hi>Moses</ns0:hi> fully in his Law given him about them on the Mount, and of which he hath written in his four last Books.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 Who <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>can rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sonably bear with.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> can have compassion on the igno<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rant <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The melting quality of the Typical High Priest is eminent<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly to be fulfilled in the Gospel one; each is to have an Aptness, Disposition, and a Sufficiency of it by the Institution of God, for his Ministrations for manner as well as for matter, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 2.18. and 4.15. <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, strictly is <ns0:hi>to bear, suffer,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>be affected in measure,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>suffer moderately</ns0:hi> with the failings of others, in such a degree as is necessary to incline, as far as he is able, to succour, help and comfort those who are in misery: it notes Sympathy, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 2.18. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 12.15. and a suffering with them, yet so regulated by the Divine Rule, as not to ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tend it unto unfit Subjects, nor in an undue Measure, lest it unfits him for ministring for them. But the great High-Priest excelleth in this, and is not bound to our measures, but sinlesly over-abounds in it, to such as sin <ns0:hi>for want of Know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledg of their Duty, unwittingly,</ns0:hi> and without any forecast, for which the Law provided a Sacrifice, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 4.2. <ns0:hi>Num.</ns0:hi> 15.24, to 30.</ns0:note>, and on them that are not out of the way <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> a Metaphor borrowed from <ns0:hi>Travellers gone out of their way</ns0:hi>; by which are understood such Sinners as are <ns0:hi>misled by Infirmity or violence of Temptation,</ns0:hi> and so offend God by their Opinions or Practices; for the Expiation of such were those Sacrifices appointed, <ns0:hi>Lev. ch.</ns0:hi> 5.6, 7. but then they were such as were sensible of their sins, confessed them, and begged for pardon, of whom the High-Priest was to be compassionate; but not of presumptuous and capital Sinners, who were unfit Subjects of God's Mercy or Man's: there being no Sacrifices provided for such, but they were to die without Mercy, <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 15.30, 31. comp. <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 22.14. God's Altar it self is no Protection to them, 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2.28, 31. Such sins of Infirmity which the Levitical High Priest was liable to himself, was he to be compassionate of.</ns0:note>, for that <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 7.28.</ns0:note> he himself also is compassed with in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />firmity <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">For that he was beset with Infirmity, Sin, Ignorance, Error, and Disobedience; infirm in respect of Duty and Sacrifice, which was by reason of its weakness to be repeated yearly, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 10.1, 11. and of the same infirm Nature liable to the Griefs and Miseries of his Brethren both in Soul and Body. All these did surround and lie about him; he was Sin and Weakness all over, and therefore should be the more feeling of his Bre<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thren's States, and more careful and ready to sacrifice and intercede for himself and them. But our great High-Priest hath all the sense of these, but no sin, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 4.15.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:551" />3 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Lev. 9.7. Chap. 7.27.</ns0:note> And by reason hereof he ought as for the people <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">This Connection demonstrates the infirmity of the Legal High Priest: <ns0:hi>For this</ns0:hi> their Infirmity, Sins of Ignorance and Error. He was <ns0:hi>obliged</ns0:hi> to his Work by the express Law of God, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> ch. 1. It is a Rule for what the Priests ought to do, and so is the whole Book to which they are to be punctually obedient, even to <ns0:hi>sacrifice</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>particular Sinners</ns0:hi> in the Church, as they were guilty and brought their Sacrifice, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> ch. 4. and for the <ns0:hi>whole Church</ns0:hi> of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> on the <ns0:hi>Atonement-day,</ns0:hi> Lev. 16.15 to 34.</ns0:note>, so also for himself to offer for sins <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">He had also his proper Sacrifice for his own Sins commonly, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 4.3. extraordinarily on the day of A<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tonement annually, <ns0:hi>Lev.</ns0:hi> 16.1, 6 to 15. It is <ns0:hi>not necessary to a Priest to be a Sinner, but it is to be merciful. Adam</ns0:hi> offered Praiers and Praises to his Creator for himself and <ns0:hi>Eve</ns0:hi> in In<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nocency; but since the Fall our Lord Jesus Christ is the only High-Priest without sin, and yet most merciful, as well as most sensible of the Sins and Miseries of penitent believing Sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ners. He offers up the Sacrifice to God truly propitiatory, as his Types did the typical ones, and procured the Pardon which God promised to give upon his so sacrificing to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chro. 26.18.</ns0:note> And no man taketh this honour unto himself <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">This connecteth the last thing describing the the typical Levitical Priesthood <ns0:hi>their Call to it.</ns0:hi> Not any Person whatso<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ever hath, or can <ns0:hi>lawfully</ns0:hi> take to himself the honourable Office of an High Priest, so as to be the Author or End of it. Many have usurped this Office, and others have distributed it contrary to God's Law, whose Priesthood, Offerings, and Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nistry are no true ones, especially where Men are <ns0:hi>self-offici<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ating,</ns0:hi> corruptly managing of it, as <ns0:hi>Eli</ns0:hi>'s Sons and <ns0:hi>Ieroboam</ns0:hi>'s Priests, or self-benefiting by it, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2.13. &c. and <ns0:hi>Mich.</ns0:hi> 3.11. This was so honourable an Office as it was united to the Prince<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dom in Melchisedeck and Jethro.</ns0:note>, but he that is called of God, <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Exod. 28.1. 1 Chro. 23.13.</ns0:note> as <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> Aaron <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He that is according to God's Law (the Author of this Priesthood, its Work and Success) qualified in himself, separated from others, and actually honoured by God with it, he ought to take this Office and execute his Work in it to God's Glory, depending on him for his Blessing. <ns0:hi>Aaron</ns0:hi> is the particular Instance of the Divine Call to this Office. God separated his Tribe, Fa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mily, and Person for his Service in the room of the first-born: God qualified him for it, intailed the High Priesthood to his Seed and Off-spring with the subordinate Priesthood. He so<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lemnly consecrated him by <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> confirmed him in his Work by Fire from heaven at his first Sacrifice, and vindicates his own Call of him to it by the blossoming Rod, and destroying the Rivals with him for it, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 28.29, 40. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 3.16, 17. and 17.5.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 So also Christ glorified not himself to be made an high priest <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">The Spirit now draws the Parallel, and shews, that what<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />soever is requisite in God's High Priest, is transcendently ful<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />filled in the Lord Jesus Christ, the Infirmities of his Types which were accidental to the Office excepted. He begins the Parallel in his Call to it, <ns0:hi>God-Man,</ns0:hi> the great Gospel-High-Priest anointed to this Office in the Flesh with the Holy Ghost, was not tainted with Ambition, neither did usurp this Honour and Dignity, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 8.54. tho there never was Person qualified for it, or deserved it like him. He never did intrude him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self upon the Office, or take the Sacerdotal Power to him, whatever others have done, and usurped it.</ns0:note>: but he that said unto him <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">But God the Father bespeaketh him, and calleth him to this high Office, as he did <ns0:hi>Aaron:</ns0:hi> He chose him, separated, sent and anointed him for it. No less Person than the eternal <ns0:hi>Iehovah</ns0:hi> could constitute and invest him in what was so high for Dignity, so glorious for Power; he did by speaking commissionate him for it, and did publish and testifie the Constitution, glorifying him in it, as is testified, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 2.7.</ns0:note>, Thou art my Son <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Thou,</ns0:hi> is not <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>Christ,</ns0:hi> as is interpreted, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.5. and <ns0:hi>Acts</ns0:hi> 13.33. <ns0:hi>art my only begotten Son,</ns0:hi> my natural Son, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 1.14, 18. The first-born of God, <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 89.27. comp. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 8.29. <ns0:hi>Colos.</ns0:hi> 1.18. As his Son, the Father could appoint him<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> to what calling he pleased. By his Primogeniture he had right to the Priest<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hood and Kingship; and to these doth the Father call him, as who would not be denied by him: From Eternity he had a Right and Title to this Office, but his solemn Investiture in it was</ns0:note>, to day have I begot<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten thee <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">on <ns0:hi>the Resurrection-day,</ns0:hi> then was he begotten to it; not only dedicated as <ns0:hi>Hannah</ns0:hi> did <ns0:hi>Samuel</ns0:hi> to the Priesthood, but solemnly after his consecration by his own Blood to it, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 9, 10, 11, 12, 23, 24. comp. <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.4. was he by the Father proclaimed to be the Son-Mediator, King, Priest, and Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />phet, and made to enter the Holy of Holiest in Heaven, and to sit down there on his Father's Right Hand, invested with Glory and Power for the Execution of his Offices, and this of his Priesthood in special, which he is daily fulfilling with him by his Intercession; see <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 7.23, 28. and 9.24. comp. <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 2.8.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">6 As he saith also in another <ns0:hi>place,</ns0:hi> 
                  <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 7.17.</ns0:note> Thou <ns0:hi>art</ns0:hi> a priest for ever <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">The Spirit proves his Call and Investiture into this Office, its Confirmation to him for ever by another Testimony of the Father about it, penn'd by <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> Psalm 110.4. and ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tified to be so by the Lord himself, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 22.41 to 45. that he as Man was <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Son, as God-Man, <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi>'s Lord, and the grand Officer to atone God by his Sacrifice for Sinners, and to interceed for him. By this Word of God to him was he invested with the most glorious Priesthood, and set<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led in that which he must execute for ever, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 7.24. ha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ving no Successor in it,</ns0:note>, after the order of Melchi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sedec <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">which Order was a singular and most excellent one; such as <ns0:hi>Aaron</ns0:hi>'s did but imperfectly sha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dow to us. It was a Royal Priesthood God installed him in, such as was <ns0:hi>Melchisedeck</ns0:hi>'s, largely described, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 7. This was by God the Father revealed to <ns0:hi>David,</ns0:hi> and prophesied by him to the Church, but actually fulfilled as to Proclamation and Inauguration at his Ascension into the Holy of Holiest in Hea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ven, where he actually in the Flesh doth officiate and mini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ster in it.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Who in the days of his flesh <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Here Christ is parallel'd in his Nature, Work and Com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />passions, to his Types, and is set above them: He was taken out of Men, as his Type was, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1. He was made Flesh, and dwelt among us in the human Nature, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 1.14. He had his Days numbred, and his Time set for his being and Ministry beneath, doing and suffering the Will of God here in a State of Humiliation, Frailty and Mortality; which Infirmi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ties attending his Flesh, are now put off for ever, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 2.14.</ns0:note>, when he had <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Joh. 17.1. &c.</ns0:note> offered up prayers and supplications <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">He performed his Service and Offering to God, as his Types, for the Men for whom he was ordained, such as he delighted in; his Prayers represented his inward Desires to God for what he needed, and was necessary in our behalf to be obtained, a Sacrifice fit to be offered by him, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 13.15. comp. 1 <ns0:hi>Pet.</ns0:hi> 2.5. <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> a Word but this once used in the New Testament; its Root signifieth an <ns0:hi>Olive Branch</ns0:hi> which Petitioners carried in their Hands; an Emblem <ns0:hi>of the vehement desire of such Supplicants of a peaceful Answer or Return to their Praiers.</ns0:hi> These of Christ were the most fervent Supplica<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tions flowing from a deeply afflicted Soul in a prostrate Body, when he was preparing for the offering up his Soul a Sacrifice for Sin, when he was in the Garden, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 22.40, 46. in his Agony, and when actually offering it on the Cross, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27.46. These were the Prayers of God-Man the Go<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spel-High-Priest,</ns0:note> with strong crying, and tears <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">put up by him unto God the Father, who is essentially good and powerful, willing and able to hear and answer his Supplications, the Fountain of all Mercy, Blessing, and Help, who could deliver him from, and save him in the greatest Dangers, so as none of those which encompassed him should hurt him, no not <ns0:hi>Death.</ns0:hi> For he was de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />livered from the evils which were far more dreadful to him than Death it self, and which were to exercise him both before and at the hour of Death. Those deadly Temptations which he underwent in his Agony and on the Cross, and from which he chargeth the Disciples to pray, that both he and they might be kept, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 26.37, 38. Those deadly Stings in his Soul, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 41. <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 14.38. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 22.40, 46. such Conflicts as his Father supported him under, carried him through, and gave him the Victory over all that Curse and Power that might do him or his mystical Body hurt. It was this Death of Deaths that did terrifie him. As for the other he chearfully underwent it, resigned his Spirit to his Father, trusted his Body in his Treasury, and was so far from being swallowed up by it, that he was gloriously risen from it.</ns0:note>, unto him that was able to save him from death <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Evident in his Agony in the mighty Groans that his Soul poured out then when he praied more earnestly, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 22.44. that which made him sweat through his Flesh congealed Clots of Blood, squeezed by his Agony out of his Body, which made him weep and cry loudly; his Voice as well as his Soul was stretched out in Prayer; the like was exercised by him in his Conflict on the Cross, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27.46. How bit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter was his Passion to him? How fervent, importunate and loud his Prayers? How did it break through the Cloud where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />with God covered his Face then? <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 22. represents in Prophesie what was now fulfilled, <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 15.34, 37. <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 23.46. It was in making satisfaction to the Justice of God for us that these were exercised to shew his inward Compassions to us, and to secure Sustentation for us in our Sufferings by Temptations, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 2.17, 18. and 4.15, 16.</ns0:note>, and was heard, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>for his piety.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> 
                  <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Joh. 12.27.</ns0:note> in that he feared <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">The Effi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cacy of these mighty Prayers and Supplications is evident by their reaching God's Ear, and procuring his Help for him. He was <ns0:hi>helped, delivered, saved,</ns0:hi> so the <ns0:hi>Septuagint</ns0:hi> use this Word in the Old Testament, putting <ns0:hi>bearing</ns0:hi> for <ns0:hi>helping,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>saving</ns0:hi> as in <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> 55.16, 17, 18. and 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 18.31. <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, this <ns0:hi>is the right acception</ns0:hi> strictly read; for as a thing is truly apprehended, it stirreth up <ns0:hi>Fear.</ns0:hi> This Word hath in Scripture-use two senses, 1. <ns0:hi>From the thing feared,</ns0:hi> by a Metonymie, <ns0:hi>Fear</ns0:hi> being put for that which works it, which was not here <ns0:hi>Death</ns0:hi> simply, for that he suffered, but what he was more afraid of than Death, <ns0:hi>viz. from the fear of being by his Temptations burried into diffidence of his Father, impatience in his Agony, or despair at the Eclipse in his Death; which the Devil design'd.</ns0:hi> As to this his Father did hear, answer, and help him, in his Agony sent his Angel to strengthen him, <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 22.43. and which he perfected for him at the end of his Passion, when he breathed out his Soul triumphantly into his Father's Hands, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 27.46, 50. and <ns0:hi>Mark</ns0:hi> 15.37, 39. <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 19.28, 29, 30. Or, 2ly. <ns0:hi>From the Fear,</ns0:hi> that godly Fear and Care in him not to displease God in any thing he did or suffered; this was a proper cause of his Acceptance, and his Prayer being heard, and his Deliverance, which is becoming the Mediator. This is a Truth, and may be admitted; but it seemeth especially to refer to the former by his Prevalency, against which by Prayer he defeated the Devil, was made <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ee<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ingly sensible of his Temptations, shewed himsef compassed with Infirmities, tho not with sinful ones, and as our High-Priest was rendred pitiful and compassionate to us under our Temptations, so as to intercede for us above, as he did pray for himself on Earth, and to procure for us Succour un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der, and Deliverance from them.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:552" />8 Though he were a son, yet learned he obe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dience by the things which he suffered <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">He fulfilled his Type in the end; for tho he were God the <ns0:hi>Son</ns0:hi> incarnate in a nearer and more excellent Relation to the Father, than any Angel, or any High-Priest among Men His Types, being all Servants to his Father and him; God's Son by eternal Generation as to his Deity, by Conception from the Holy Ghost by the Virgin as to his Humanity, who for his worth might have been exempted from such Bur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dens, yet did God teach him (not as if he wanted it at any Time) by what he imposed and commanded him, and <ns0:hi>he learnt</ns0:hi> by what he did agree and covenant to perform <ns0:hi>Active Obedi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ence</ns0:hi> to God's Will, fulfilling all Righteousness, being for his Person, and doing for his Work to a Tittle what God required from him, but especially <ns0:hi>Passive Obedience,</ns0:hi> by his experience knowing what it meant, freely subjecting himself to his State of Humiliation, <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 2.6, 7, 8. enduring all the Indignities and Sufferings for Sinners from his Birth to his Death, even the most vile and cursed. This the Father injoined and commanded him, and he did obey it; read <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 53. He who offered Prayers for himself, as an High-Priest offered himself a Sacrifice for us, as ours. By this did he finish his Father's Will intirely, experimentally, feelingly, knowing how diffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cult Patience under the Cross is, and how to pity us under all our Sufferings.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 2.10.</ns0:note> And being made perfect <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">As to the powerful Execution of his Office, this God-Man exceed's his Types; for having consummated all the Work to which he was designed dy his doing, suffering, dying, rising, and ascending into Heaven in the human Nature, he perfected the Work of Redemption, and consecrated himself to his Office.</ns0:note>, he became the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">By this was he constituted, made, and declared by his Father to be, not an <ns0:hi>Instrument</ns0:hi> as all his Types were, but the <ns0:hi>Cause efficient</ns0:hi> meritorious and exemplar of Salvation, by his Sacrifice satisfying God's Justice, meriting and effecting Reconciliation and Justification for Sinners; and on his Ascen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sion sends forth the Holy Ghost to qualifie them for the Re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ception of his Benefits, by working in them what he requires, and on their Application to him, he, as their High Priest, pleads the Merit of his Blood, and intercedes for their Justi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fication and <ns0:hi>Salvation,</ns0:hi> which is the freeing them from all Evil criminal and penal, Sin, and whatever it subjecteth them to in this World, or that which is to come; and instating them into all the heavenly Priviledges promised in the Covenant of Grace, Righteousness, Holiness, Heirship to, and Life and Glory with God, and to be safe in the Possession of them all, not for Time only, but for Eternity. This efficient Cause produceth this only to the duly qualified Subject: Mankind is rendred salvable by the Obedience and Sacrifice of this High-Priest; but it is only to penitent believing Sinners that he doth communicate this, and for whom he effects it; those who will intirely submit themselves to Christ as a Lord and King, and be loyal to him and obey him, as well as to a Priest or a Saviour, continuing his faithful Subjects to the end, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 3.16, 18, 36. comp. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 10.22.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 Called of God an high priest after the or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der of Melchisedeck <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">His Constitution by God the Father in his Office, maketh it so effectual; he was solemnly proclaimed and declared to be what God had constituted him. <ns0:hi>God nameth or calleth things as they are,</ns0:hi> and as he hath made them; and this was done open<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly, and with the most illustrious Solemnity at his Ascension into Heaven, when God sate him down on his Right Hand in the presence of all the surrounding Angels, who did all submit to him as their Head and King, and acknowledge him as the great Royal High Priest of God, as was foretold, <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 110.1, 2. which Words of the Psalmist the Spirit further explaineth in <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 7. where he proves this Gospel-High-Priest to be of a more excellent order than <ns0:hi>Aaron</ns0:hi>'s, even like that of <ns0:hi>Melchisedeck</ns0:hi> which it exceedeth, and which must last for ever.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Of whom we have many things to say, and hard to be uttered <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">The Spirit here digresseth from discoursing further of the Priesthood of Christ, that he may fit these Hebrews to apprehend and improve it when he shall return to it, <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 7. He beginneth with a Reproof, which takes up the remain<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der of the Chapter, aed enters on it artificially from the Doctrine delivered of Christ's Priesthood, insinuating the Difficulty of its Reception by them: <ns0:gap reason="foreign">

                     </ns0:gap> 
                     <ns0:hi>of whom,</ns0:hi> some would make to refer to <ns0:hi>Melchisedeck,</ns0:hi> but by what followeth in this and <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 7. it can be spoken of none but of Christ the Truth of that Type, who was made an High-Priest after that order. And of him the Apostle was filled by the Spirit with mat<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ter, as <ns0:hi>Elihu</ns0:hi> speaks, <ns0:hi>Iob</ns0:hi> 32.18. Much he had to say of this Mystery, which was most excellent and weighty, and which a few words could not express; for it was <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, not unutterable in it self, or difficult <ns0:hi>for him to open and interpret,</ns0:hi> but for them to understand.</ns0:note>, seeing ye are dull of hearing <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Because the Ears of their Mind were not created nor proportioned to it: they were Babes and Children in Understanding; the difficulty was in themselves, not in the Word or Mystery: Their intellective Faculty was slow to discern, perceive, and judge of this Doctrine, and their Hearts were averse to it, being so conceit<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed concerning the Levitical Priesthood; such were the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stles at the first, <ns0:hi>Iohn</ns0:hi> 16.12.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 For when for the time ye ought to be teachers <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">The Conviction of this fault in their Understanding and Will, is by the Spirit demonstrated; for their dullness proceeded from their neglect of God's means of Know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge, and so were inexcusable; they <ns0:hi>had time and means enough</ns0:hi> of improving in the knowledg of this Gospel-Do<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ctrine of Christ's Priesthood, and to have gained in them the abilities of <ns0:hi>Teachers</ns0:hi> of their Families, fellow Christians and Neighbours both from the Law of <ns0:hi>Moses,</ns0:hi> and the o<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther Scriptures, and by the Teaching of Christ and his Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stles.</ns0:note>, ye have need that one teach you again which <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> the first principles <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Yet such was their negligence and idleness, that their Knowledge was diminished and lost, and they faln off to the Old <ns0:hi>Mosaical</ns0:hi> Oeconomy of Priesthood, Ceremonies and Services, so as they had need again to be taught and in<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />structed by others, which are the <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of God's Ora<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cles in the Scriptures. Such things as are the <ns0:hi>first in or<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />der,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>first</ns0:hi> to be taught and learnt, the very <ns0:hi>Fundamental Principles</ns0:hi> of Christianity, without the knowledg of which none can be saved, and on which all others do depend. They are so stiled by a Metaphor, signifying such a state of <ns0:hi>this in the Scripture, as the Elements have in natural bodies which they compound</ns0:hi>; or, like <ns0:hi>Elements of Speech,</ns0:hi> which must be first attained before there can be either an Understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, Speaking or Writing of a Language; they are the foundation upon which a System of the Christian Religion is raised, see <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 6.1. which Principles lie dispersed in the New-Testament, and are summed up in those Antient Creeds which are agreeable to our Saviour's Words.</ns0:note> of the ora<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cles of God <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, such Oracles or Revelations of God's Mind about the way of our Salvation, which he hath made to us by his Son our High-Priest, and which he brought from Heaven with him, and taught himself, as <ns0:hi>ch.</ns0:hi> 1.1, 2. and hath by the Inspiration of his Spirit of Persons, chosen on purpose by him, penned them eminently in the Scriptures of the New-Testament, not excluding those of the Old-Te<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stament which are unvailed, opened and made glorious in them, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 3.2.</ns0:note>, and are become such as have need of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">1 Cor. 3.1, 2, 3.</ns0:note> milk, and not of strong meat <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">These <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi> had so greatly forgot<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ten these first Principles, that they were become meer Babes and Infants in Knowledg, they needed <ns0:hi>the first and weakest Spiritual Food,</ns0:hi> metaphorically stiled <ns0:hi>Milk,</ns0:hi> the most plain and easy Truths of the Gospel, such as they may un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand, and give light to others; not the Beggarly Ele<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments of <ns0:hi>Iudaism,</ns0:hi> as they are stiled, <ns0:hi>Gal.</ns0:hi> 4.3, 9. and <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 2.8, 20. which would keep them ignorant Babes in the Word of Righteousness, and unfit them for the under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />standing and digesting the <ns0:hi>stronger Food</ns0:hi> of the higher and more excellent Doctrines of the Gospel concerning Christ's Priesthood; such a Babe was <ns0:hi>Nicodemus,</ns0:hi> though a Master in <ns0:hi>Israel, Iohn</ns0:hi> 3.10, 12.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 For every one that useth milk <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The Spirit proves these <ns0:hi>Hebrews</ns0:hi> such Infants by descri<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bing the state of them, and of their contrary, and tacite<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly appling it to them under a Metaphor or Allegory start<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed by him before.                      </ns0:gap>, <ns0:hi>not truly knowing,</ns0:hi> not <ns0:hi>proving nor experiencing,</ns0:hi> never exercised or practised in the <ns0:hi>Word of Righteousness, the Gospel-Doctrine,</ns0:hi> which is in it self an Eternal certain Truth, the Revelation of the Righteousness of God to Faith, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 1.16; 17. And the instrumental conveye<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> of it to Faith; a perfect Rule of Righteousness, making Christians conform exactly to the Mind and Will of God, and so reaching the state of strong and perfect ones, <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 1.25. to 29.</ns0:note>: for he is a Babe <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He is <ns0:hi>but a new-born Christian,</ns0:hi> a Child in Christ's School, one that cannot be experienced in the Perfections of God's Word, because he is weak in Knowledge, Ignorant and unconstant like an Infant, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 14.20. compare <ns0:hi>Ephes.</ns0:hi> 4.14.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:552" />14 But strong meat belongeth to them that are of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>perfect.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> full age <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">But those <ns0:hi>great deep and high Mysteries of the Gospel</ns0:hi> con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cerning Christ's Natures, their Hypostatical Union, his Offi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ces, his actual fulfilling all his Types in the Old Testa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment both Personal and Mystical, with the Prophesies of his Gospel-Church-State, and his Mediatory Kingdom, <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> these are the strong Meat and Food of <ns0:hi>grown Christians,</ns0:hi> who have reached some maturity in the knowledg of these Gospel-Mysteries, and are of a full Age in Understanding, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 2.6. and 14.20. and <ns0:hi>Phil.</ns0:hi> 3.15.                         <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>

                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> strictly notes such an <ns0:hi>exercise as Wrestlers use for a Victory with all their Might and Strength, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing trained up to it by long Exercise.</ns0:hi> The Spiritual organs or faculties of Christians are well instructed, practised, made apt and ready, as the external ones are, for their proper work.</ns0:note> to discern both good and evil <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> for the <ns0:hi>discerning</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>differencing</ns0:hi> things, so as the Mind discerns what Doctrine is true, and what is false by the Word of Righteousness, and the Will chooseth what is Good, and refuseth what is Evil; the af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fections love Good, and hate Evil; as the senses external can by Exercise discern what Food is gustful, pleasing and wholesom for the Person, and what is nauseous and un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />wholesom.                      </ns0:gap>, by a gracious habit of Wisdom and Knowledg infused and perfected by long study, practice and exercise of them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves in the Word of Righteousness, by which they are able to apprehend and improve the highest Doctrines of the Mystery of Christ.</ns0:note>
